title: Wealth, earned and shared
hook: money is not evil; clinging to it and hoarding it are

segments.voice: Yesterday, work as worship: Lalo's bread and Bhago's feast, and kirat, honest work. Your line: work is worship.

Is money bad? Ask that at a dinner table and watch it split. Somebody says money ruins everything it touches. Somebody else says try paying rent with good intentions. Both have a point, and both are a little stuck. Honest work, done well, sometimes earns more than bread. A shop does well. A farm has a good year. A salary goes up. Then the question isn't how to earn. It's what to do with what you've earned, and what it starts doing to you.
screen: `IS MONEY BAD?` → `THE TABLE SPLITS.` → `WHAT DO YOU DO WITH WHAT YOU EARN?`

segments.voice: Money isn't the enemy. The salok we met yesterday honors the one who eats what they earn by their own work. Sikh life has room for farms, shops, businesses and savings; the householder needs a roof. So where does the trouble start? In Raag Asa, in hymns tradition links to Babar's invasion, Guru Nanak looks at wealth with clear eyes. In paraphrase: for the sake of this wealth, many were ruined and disgraced; it isn't piled up without wrongdoing, and it doesn't go along with anyone when they die. The problem isn't the coin. It's the clinging, the piling up, the wealth that has to be guarded and that guards you back. Now the other half of yesterday's line. That salok doesn't stop at earning. It says: and gives some of it from their hand. The hand that earns is meant to open. Sikhs call this sharing vand chhakna, and tradition adds dasvandh, setting aside a tenth share of what you earn for the community and for those in need; you met it in year one. Gifts like this can help feed the langar. Earning without sharing tightens the fist. Sharing without honest earning gives away what was never yours. Together, money moves through a life instead of sitting on it. A hand that earns and then opens isn't owned by what it holds. Earned and shared.
screen: `EARNING IS NOT SHAMEFUL.` · `IT DOESN'T GO ALONG AT DEATH.` · `THE HAND THAT EARNS SHOULD OPEN.` · `MONEY MOVES THROUGH, NOT SITS ON.` · then, large: `EARNED AND SHARED.`

segments.voice: Hold the picture of what you earned or received this week without adding it up, and think of one place a little of it could go that isn't you: a food bank, a gurdwara's langar, a neighbor who's short this month. Rest your hand open on your lap while you breathe, and notice what it feels like to plan to let go of something. If you pray, hold the gift with Waheguru.
Wealth. Not evil in itself; earned honestly, it is meant to be shared, and it does not go along with anyone at the end. Today's word.
Your line: earned and shared. The hand that earns is meant to open. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-one, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of vand chhakna, sharing what one earns, and tradition describes dasvandh, setting aside a share of income, for the community and those in need, including the langar.

chat.says: Does Sikh teaching say having money is bad?
options: No. Honest earning is fine; the trouble is clinging. The hand that earns should open.
Yes. Guru Nanak says a person on the path should own nothing at all, ever.
No. In Sikh teaching wealth goes along with you after death as merit.
